explanations.explanation: That's the ask, baker. The Pharisees and Sadducees come and test Jesus by asking Him to show them a sign from heaven (Matthew 16:1). Notice they aren't just asking. The text says they came to test Him. I think that's a very different way to knock on a door.

Good guess, since a letter is a very official thing to ask for. But the text says they ask Jesus to show them a sign from heaven (Matthew 16:1). No mail involved. They came to test Him, and they wanted something to see.

A scroll sounds religious enough, I'll give you that. But the Pharisees and Sadducees don't ask for one. They ask Him to show them a sign from heaven (Matthew 16:1). The text says they came to test Him.

That's right, friend. Jesus says that in the morning they say, “Today it will be stormy, for the sky is red and overcast.” (Matthew 16:3). Red sky at night, fair weather. Red and overcast in the morning, storm. They read the sky like someone who glances at the clouds and grabs an umbrella before the first drop.

This one is true, friend. Jesus says they say in the morning, “Today it will be stormy, for the sky is red and overcast.” (Matthew 16:3). It's right there in the verse. They read the sky just fine, and that's the point He's about to make.

Yes, baker! Jesus says, “You know how to interpret the appearance of the sky, but not the signs of the times.” (Matthew 16:3). They could read clouds like a pro. The bigger signs were right in front of them, and they didn't read those.

Moses, sent to bring Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 3:10), is a fair name to think of with these men, since the law was given through Moses (John 1:17). But Jesus doesn't say that here. He says they know how to interpret the appearance of the sky, “…but not the signs of the times.” (Matthew 16:3).

The sky is the right neighborhood, friend. But Jesus talks about the sky at evening and in the morning, red or overcast (Matthew 16:2-3). What they can't interpret is “…the signs of the times.” (Matthew 16:3). My own night sky is full of cookie-box stars, and even I can't read those like a forecast.

That's it, baker. Jesus says none will be given “…except the sign of Jonah.” (Matthew 16:4). Jonah was a prophet who ran from God's call to go to Nineveh (Jonah 1:1-3). Jesus doesn't spell out the sign in this passage, so I'll leave it right there.

Moses, sent to bring Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 3:10), is a big name, so I see why he came to mind. But Jesus says none will be given “…except the sign of Jonah.” (Matthew 16:4). Jonah was a prophet who ran from God's call to go to Nineveh (Jonah 1:1-3).

Elijah was a prophet (1 Kings 18:36) with some big moments, so that guess has some flavor. But Jesus doesn't name him here. He says none will be given “…except the sign of Jonah.” (Matthew 16:4). One name, one sign.
Close, but no. The verse ends with, “Then He left them and went away.” (Matthew 16:4). He doesn't stay to keep debating. He says His piece and walks off, and I think that says plenty.
That's right, friend. Matthew 16:4 says, “Then He left them and went away.” No debate club, no second round. He says what He says and goes.
Bread it is, baker. Matthew 16:5 says the disciples forgot to take bread. Now, I've forgotten the baking powder before, and I live in a bakery. It happens to the best of us.
Nets make sense, since some of the disciples were fishermen (Matthew 4:18). But that's not what the text says they forgot. Matthew 16:5 says they forgot to take bread.
A cloak is an easy thing to forget, and I bet you'd feel it fast once you got to the other side. But the text says nothing about cloaks. It says the disciples forgot to take bread (Matthew 16:5).

Yes, friend. The disciples discuss it among themselves and conclude, “It is because we did not bring any bread.” (Matthew 16:7). Jesus says leaven, and their minds go straight to the bread basket. I think we've all heard one word and run the wrong direction with it.

This one is true, friend. The disciples discuss it and conclude, “It is because we did not bring any bread.” (Matthew 16:7). They heard "leaven" and thought about the bread they forgot. The text says that's what they decided.
That's right, baker. The text says Jesus was “Aware of their conversation…” (Matthew 16:8). They were talking among themselves, and He knew what they were saying. Then He speaks up.
Not quite, friend. Matthew 16:8 says Jesus was “Aware of their conversation…” They were talking among themselves, and He knew what they were saying. Then He speaks up.

Loaves, baker! Jesus asks, “Do you not remember the five loaves for the five thousand…?” and then “Or the seven loaves for the four thousand…” (Matthew 16:9-10). He asks how many basketfuls they gathered each time. He brings up those loaves right when they're debating having no bread (Matthew 16:8).

Jesus did heal people (Matthew 15:30-31), so I get why healings came up. But that's not what He asks about here. He says, “Do you not remember the five loaves for the five thousand…?” (Matthew 16:9). Then it's the seven loaves for the four thousand (Matthew 16:10).

Jesus did teach in parables (Matthew 13:3), so that's a fair thought. But in this moment He's asking about something they could count. He says, “Do you not remember the five loaves for the five thousand…?” (Matthew 16:9), then the seven loaves for the four thousand (Matthew 16:10).

That's right, friend. Jesus says, “How do you not understand that I was not telling you about bread?” (Matthew 16:11). Plain as day, and they'd missed it. I once stamped a whole batch upside down, so I won't throw stones.

This one is true, friend. Jesus says, “How do you not understand that I was not telling you about bread?” (Matthew 16:11). The bread worry was a detour. He had a different warning in mind, and He says it again right after.

Teaching, baker, and that's the word. Matthew 16:12 says they understood He was not telling them to beware of the leaven used in bread, “…but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees.” Leaven is something I know from my bakery, and I never once thought of it as teaching. Jesus did.

Wealth sounds like a sensible guess, friend, but that's not the one. Matthew 16:12 says they understood He was warning them “…of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees.” It was about what those men taught, not their money. If it were about my money, this would be a very short warning, because my price tag said 25 cents.

Prayers is a thoughtful guess, baker, but it's not in the verse. Matthew 16:12 says they understood He meant “…the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees.” Not the bread, and not their prayers. The word is teaching, plain as a cookie with no sprinkles.
